title: Vitrifi Cortex Portal: Multi-Tenant Wholesale Broadband Engineering — Audio Guide

chapters.title: What Cortex Portal was
chapters.script: Vitrifi was a software company building Cortex Portal, a multi-tenant platform for the United Kingdom wholesale broadband market. The company has since shut down, so this is a retrospective on a system I worked in for nearly four years. Cortex Portal sat in the middle of the broadband supply chain. On one side were the network owners who physically run fibre into the ground, the wholesale carriers like CityFibre, Openreach, and BT. On the other side were the internet service providers who actually sell broadband to homes and businesses. Cortex Portal was the operational software those providers used to discover where service was available, place orders, and drive each connection through to activation. The product was sold as software as a service. Every provider was a separate tenant, with its own users, its own data, and its own branding, all running on shared infrastructure. That single fact, multi-tenancy, shaped almost every technical decision in the codebase, from how we connected to databases to how we checked permissions on every request. The domain itself is unglamorous but genuinely hard. A broadband order is not a shopping cart. It is a long-running, stateful workflow that can take days or weeks, that depends on third-party systems we did not control, and that fails in dozens of partial ways. An address might not have fibre yet. An appointment with the carrier might slip. A network device might provision but fail its configuration. The software had to model all of that honestly rather than pretend the happy path was the only path. My role was full-stack engineer, and over the life of the project I made close to five thousand commits. I was one of the primary contributors, not the only one, and I want to be precise about that. What I owned end to end were the form and validation systems, large parts of the subscriber and contact management, the type-safety story across the frontend, the end-to-end test infrastructure, and a steady stream of security hardening. Across this narration I will walk through the architecture as it really was, and then through the parts I personally built, with enough detail that you could ask me hard questions about any of it. The goal is not a highlight reel. The goal is an accurate account of a real production system and the engineering judgement that went into it.

chapters.title: The ordering lifecycle
chapters.script: To understand the code you have to understand the order. In Cortex Portal the central object was the service order, and it had a life. It began as a new service order, often called an NSO internally, which is a request to bring broadband to a specific address for a specific subscriber on a specific product. Before an order could even exist, the address had to be qualified. We had a dedicated addressing service whose entire job was to answer questions about geography and availability. Given a postcode or a unique property reference number, the United Kingdom standard identifier for a property, it could say whether the network reached that location and what speeds were possible. That qualification step mattered because everything downstream depended on it. Once an order was placed it moved through a sequence of states. It could be submitted to the wholesale carrier, accepted, rejected, or amended. After activation it did not stop being interesting. A subscriber might regrade to a faster product, suspend service, resume it, or terminate entirely. Each of those was its own workflow with its own validation, its own permissions, and its own side effects on the network. The activation half of the system deserves its own mention. There was a separate application and a separate backend, the network activator, used by operations teams to drive the physical and logical provisioning. That meant booking appointments with carriers like CityFibre and Openreach, provisioning the optical network unit at the customer premises, the device often abbreviated as ONU, and tracking the network state as it changed. The portal side cared about the commercial order. The activator side cared about turning that order into a working line. The two had to stay consistent even though they were different services owned by different teams. What made this domain demanding was the integrations. We did not live in a closed world. We talked to external carrier systems over their own protocols and contracts, with their own identifiers and their own failure modes. A carrier appointment identifier, for example, had a very specific format that we validated with a regular expression so that a malformed value never reached the carrier. Modelling someone else's state machine inside your own, while keeping your users informed about a process that is mostly out of your hands, is one of the quietly difficult problems in this kind of software, and a lot of the engineering effort went exactly there.

chapters.title: System shape and scale
chapters.script: Cortex Portal was a single monorepo, managed with the pnpm package manager and Turborepo for task orchestration and caching. Keeping everything in one repository was a deliberate choice. The contracts between services were shared, the code generation crossed language boundaries, and a monorepo let a single change to a schema ripple out to every consumer in one commit and one review. The backend was Go. The frontend was TypeScript and React. As a rough sense of scale, there were on the order of two hundred and forty thousand lines of Go and around eighty thousand lines of TypeScript, across roughly two thousand source files. That was split across five backend services, two main frontend applications, and a set of shared frontend packages. The backend services were the GraphQL portal interface, the network activator backend, the addressing service, a tenancy service that brokered database connections, and a collateral service that handled document storage. The frontends were the operator portal and the network activator application, with an administrative surface as well. The shared packages were published inside the workspace under a cortex scope. There was a validations package, a hooks package, a user interface component package, a utilities package, and a constants package. The point of those packages was that the two applications should not reinvent the same form validation, the same error handling, or the same design tokens independently. They should import them. The testing surface was substantial. There was an end-to-end suite written with Playwright, the browser automation framework, covering real user journeys like creating and activating a new service. There were Go fuzz tests, which feed deliberately malformed input into parsers to find crashes. There were integration tests that stood up real dependencies with containers, a database, the messaging system, and the portal interface, and exercised them together. And there was a continuous integration and delivery pipeline on GitLab that linted, vetted, tested, scanned for vulnerabilities, versioned, and built container images. None of those numbers are the interesting part on their own. What they tell you is that this was not a prototype. It was a system with enough surface area that consistency had to be engineered rather than hoped for, and most of my best work was about exactly that, making a large codebase behave like it was written by one careful person rather than many people in a hurry.

chapters.title: The GraphQL core
chapters.script: The heart of the system was the portal interface, a Go service that exposed a single large GraphQL API. We used GraphQL deliberately. The frontend needed to compose very different views, an order list, a subscriber profile, a network summary, and a graph let each screen ask for exactly the data it needed without us hand-writing an endpoint per screen. The server was generated from the schema using gqlgen, a Go library that takes GraphQL schema files and produces the type-safe server scaffolding, leaving you to implement resolvers. There were dozens of schema files and a correspondingly large set of resolvers, organised by domain. There was an order resolver, a subscriber resolver, a named contact resolver, and so on. Each resolver was the place where business rules actually lived. Data lived in MongoDB, the document database, and here is where multi-tenancy showed up in the most concrete way. We did not have one shared database with a tenant column. Each tenant had its own database, and a connection manager component, which the code called connman, was responsible for handing a resolver the correct per-tenant connection based on the authenticated request. A resolver never picked a database. It asked the context for the tenant's connection and trusted that the plumbing had already isolated it. That design made cross-tenant data leakage structurally hard rather than merely discouraged. The service was also event-driven. It used the NATS messaging system, with messages defined as protocol buffers, to publish things that happened. When a user was updated, when an order changed state, the service published an event rather than calling every interested party directly. Other services subscribed. That decoupling let the activation workflows react to commercial events asynchronously without the portal interface knowing or caring who was listening. Startup of this service was itself a small lesson in real systems. It read configuration from the environment, registered tracing so requests could be followed across services, opened clients to the addressing, collateral, and tenancy services, established the messaging client with signature verification so forged events were rejected, set up a client for a carrier integration with mutual transport security, fetched the public keys needed to validate authentication tokens for every tenant, and then finally served traffic over a modern transport with a strict minimum security version. Every one of those steps existed because something in production needed it. The resolver code was the part people saw. The startup code was the part that kept it honest.

chapters.title: The other services
chapters.script: The portal interface was the largest service but it was not alone, and the way the others were built is as informative as the way it was. The network activator backend was a representational state transfer API, a REST service, built on the Echo web framework in Go. It served the operations teams who drive provisioning. Its job was to expose endpoints for network configuration, to activate and erase services on devices, and to summarise orders and network state. It authenticated with the same token scheme as the portal but mapped each tenant to its identity pool, and it both published and consumed messaging events to coordinate asynchronous work. It is worth noticing that we did not force every service to be GraphQL. The activator was request-response and operational, so a plain REST API described from an OpenAPI specification fit it better. The addressing service was different again. It was a remote procedure call service using gRPC, Google's high-performance remote procedure call framework, and unlike the rest of the system its data lived in PostgreSQL, the relational database, not MongoDB. That choice was correct. Address and network topology data is highly relational and query-heavy, with postcodes, property identifiers, and network nodes, and a relational engine with real indexes is the right tool. The queries were not handwritten ad hoc. They were generated with sqlc, a tool that turns annotated SQL into type-safe Go functions, so the database layer was compile-checked rather than stringly typed. Schema changes were managed with versioned migrations. The tenancy service was small and almost boring on purpose. Its job was to broker per-tenant database connection details to the other services. There was even a tracked task to eventually remove it and fold its responsibility elsewhere, which tells you something healthy about the team. Infrastructure that exists only to glue other things together is a liability you should be looking to retire, not a monument. The collateral service handled document storage, uploads and generated paperwork, backed by object storage in the cloud. The reason this matters is the same reason the monorepo mattered. Each service was the right shape for its problem. GraphQL where views composed many entities, REST where the surface was operational, gRPC where it was tight service-to-service traffic over a relational store. Nobody was forced into a single pattern for ideological neatness, and the contracts between them were all generated from shared schemas so the freedom did not turn into chaos.

chapters.title: Schema first development
chapters.script: If there is one idea that explains how this codebase stayed coherent at its size, it is schema-first development. Almost nothing important was written by hand twice. There were four kinds of contract, and each one generated code rather than being mirrored manually. GraphQL schema files generated the Go server types and resolver interfaces through gqlgen, and they also generated TypeScript types and React hooks for the frontend through a code generation toolchain. OpenAPI specifications generated the Go handlers and models for the REST services. Protocol buffer definitions generated the Go message types and the remote procedure call stubs. And annotated SQL generated the type-safe database access functions through sqlc. There was a generate step in the build that ran all of this in order, and a developer who changed a schema was expected to regenerate and commit the output. The reason this is worth a chapter of its own is the failure mode it removes. In a hand-synchronised system, the backend changes a field, the frontend keeps the old shape, and nothing complains until a user hits the bug in production. In a schema-first system the same change breaks the build. The TypeScript stops compiling because the generated type changed. The Go stops compiling because the resolver signature changed. The mismatch is caught at the moment it is introduced, by the person who introduced it, on their own machine, instead of by a customer weeks later. There was also a quieter benefit that I leaned on heavily in my own work. Because the frontend types were generated from the same schema as the backend, I could derive form field names and input shapes directly from the generated types instead of typing string literals. When the schema renamed a field, every form that referenced it failed to compile until it was fixed. That turned a whole class of silent runtime bugs into loud compile-time bugs. Generated code has a reputation for being ugly, and some of it was. The honest tradeoff is that you accept large generated files in version control and a slightly slower build in exchange for an entire category of integration mistake simply not being possible. On a system with this many moving parts and more than one author, that trade was overwhelmingly worth making. A great deal of my time was spent making sure the generation pipeline was actually trusted, because a code generation step that people route around by hand is worse than none at all.

chapters.title: Authorization and input safety
chapters.script: Security in Cortex Portal was not a separate module bolted on the side. It was expressed in the schema and enforced by the framework on every single request, and that is a design I came to strongly believe in. Authorization used a custom GraphQL directive. Every query and mutation that needed protection was annotated in the schema with a has-permission directive listing the permissions required, written in a resource and action style, for example read on the order resource or update on the subscriber resource. A piece of middleware implemented that directive. Before a resolver ran, the middleware compared the permissions on the authenticated request against the permissions the field declared, and if they did not match it returned an authorization error and the resolver never executed. The important property is that authorization was declarative and lived next to the field it protected, so you could read the schema and see exactly who was allowed to do what, rather than hunting through imperative checks scattered across the code. Input validation worked the same way. There was a validate directive that applied tag-based rules to input fields, things like required, or a valid email, or a value greater than zero, with custom messages. There was a validate-regex directive for pattern rules, which is how that strict carrier appointment identifier format was enforced at the edge. And there was an html directive for the rare fields that legitimately accept formatted text, like a notification body. That directive ran the input through a sanitiser using the bluemonday library with a user-generated-content policy, which strips dangerous markup and prevents cross-site scripting, the class of attack abbreviated as XSS where attacker markup runs in another user's browser. I did a meaningful amount of the work on this surface. I added the safe html scalar type and its directive, and I fixed real bugs in it, like trimming whitespace so a trailing newline from a text area did not defeat validation. The mental model I want to leave you with is this. The schema was the single place that described not just the shape of the data but the rules about it. Who can call this. What must be true about the input. What gets sanitised. Because all of that was declarative and enforced centrally, a new resolver was secure by default. You had to actively annotate it to open it up, rather than remembering to add protection you could easily forget. Secure-by-default is worth far more than secure-if-you-remember.

chapters.title: Multi tenant isolation
chapters.script: Multi-tenancy is easy to say and hard to do correctly, and Cortex Portal took the stricter path. Every internet service provider on the platform, every ISP, was a tenant, and tenants had to be isolated so completely that one provider could never see another provider's subscribers, orders, or addresses, even through a bug. Identity was handled by a managed cloud authentication service. Each tenant had its own user pool, its own population of users entirely separate from every other tenant. When a user signed in, the token they received carried the tenant context. The portal interface fetched the configuration for every tenant's pool and maintained the set of public keys needed to verify tokens, per pool, so a token could be both authenticated and attributed to the right tenant on every request. Data isolation was physical rather than logical. Instead of one shared database with a tenant identifier column on every table, which is the design where a single missing filter leaks everyone's data, each tenant had its own MongoDB database. The connection manager I mentioned earlier resolved the right database from the request's tenant and placed that connection in the request context. Resolvers read the connection from context. They did not, and structurally could not, choose a different tenant's database by forgetting a filter, because there was no shared store to forget to filter. The one place data was deliberately shared was the addressing service on PostgreSQL, where geography is genuinely common across tenants, and there isolation was enforced explicitly in the query layer. Standing a tenant up was not just a database. A new tenant needed baseline data to be usable at all. Roles had to exist, an administrator role with full permissions, an operator role, a tenant user role. Permissions had to be attached to those roles. Product offerings, order status values, and activity types had to be present. There was a seeding system that produced this consistent baseline, and I did a lot of work there, adding permissions for new resources to the right roles, seeding prospect and subscriber templates, and fixing the not-found handling around them. Seed data sounds trivial until you realise that every developer environment, every test run, and every freshly created tenant depends on it being correct and consistent. If the seed is wrong, every downstream test is testing the wrong world. Getting that boring layer right is what lets the exciting layers be trustworthy.

chapters.title: The frontend
chapters.script: The frontend was a TypeScript and React codebase, and it was built with the same seriousness as the backend rather than treated as a thin skin over the API. The main applications used React version eighteen, with React Router for navigation and Apollo Client as the GraphQL client, which gave us a normalised cache and generated hooks for every operation. The component library was Ant Design, a mature enterprise component system, which was the right call for software whose users are operations staff filling in dense forms all day rather than consumers browsing a marketing site. Styling used Emotion, a library for writing component-scoped styles in TypeScript. The build tool was Rsbuild, a modern fast bundler. The detail that mattered most was the shared packages under the cortex scope. There was a validations package holding reusable rules, things like a valid United Kingdom phone number, a valid service identifier, password strength, names. There was a hooks package with cross-application React hooks. There was a user interface package wrapping the component system with consistent theming and layout primitives. There was a utilities package, and a constants package holding error codes and shared strings. The reason this structure existed is that we had more than one application. Without shared packages, the portal and the network activator would each grow their own slightly different phone number validator and their own slightly different error display, and they would drift apart and both be subtly wrong. With shared packages there was exactly one phone number validator, tested once, used everywhere. I spent real effort consolidating things into that shared layer. One concrete example was icons. Early on, components imported icons from several different libraries in several different ways, which bloated the bundle and made the interface visually inconsistent. I built a single icon map that exported every icon the applications used, and then methodically migrated component after component to reference it, so there was one source of truth and one bundle cost. Another example was layout. The same flex container with the same gap was written by hand in dozens of components. I extracted small layout utilities, a flex gap helper, a header row helper, and replaced the duplication. None of this is glamorous. Nobody demos an icon map. But this kind of consolidation is the difference between a frontend that gets faster and more consistent as it grows and one that gets slower and more random. A large React codebase does not stay coherent by accident. It stays coherent because someone keeps deliberately pulling the shared parts back into the centre, and on this project that someone was frequently me.

chapters.title: The validation framework
chapters.script: The piece of Cortex Portal I owned most completely was the form and validation framework on the frontend, and it is the part I would most want to be asked about. Cortex Portal is, from the user's seat, an enormous collection of forms. Create a subscriber. Edit a service order. Configure a tenant application. Add a named contact. Every one of those is a form with rules, and rules that are wrong or inconsistent are not cosmetic. They block real orders or let bad data through. I architected the validation layer around two libraries working together. React Hook Form managed form state and submission efficiently, and Zod described the shape and rules of the data as a schema. The pattern was that each form defined a Zod schema once, and from that single schema we derived both the runtime validation, which actually rejects bad input, and the static TypeScript type of the form values. One declaration, two guarantees, always in step. That sounds clean stated in one sentence. The reality was a long, careful migration spanning months. The validation had started as ad hoc rules, and moving more than fifty forms onto declarative schemas without breaking live workflows was incremental surgery. On top of that I led two non-trivial dependency migrations underneath the framework, moving the schema library from its third major version to its fourth, whose syntax changed, and moving the form resolver bridge from its third major version to its fifth. Those upgrades touched every form, so they had to be done methodically, with the type checker and the test suite as the safety net rather than hope. The part I am proudest of is error handling, because that is where most form systems quietly fail. A server can reject input the client thought was fine, a duplicate value for instance. If that error just appears as a generic toast, the user has no idea which field to fix. I built a shared error handler hook that took a server error, extracted the field path from the error's structured extensions, recognised specific codes like a duplicate, and set the message on exactly the right form field with a helpful message, falling back gracefully when it could not. The result was that a backend rejection turned into a red message under the precise input that caused it, not a vague banner. That single piece of plumbing, unglamorous as it is, probably removed more daily user frustration than any feature I shipped.

chapters.title: Subscribers and named contacts
chapters.script: I want to tell one story in detail, because it shows how a small-sounding rule reaches through every layer of a real system. In Cortex Portal a subscriber is the customer on a broadband order, and a named contact is an authorised representative tied to that subscriber, someone allowed to act on the account. The deceptively hard rule was identity. Sometimes the customer is a person, with a first name and a last name. Sometimes the customer is a company, with a company name and no personal name. The system could not demand both, because for a residential customer there is no company, and it could not demand neither, because then you have an order attached to nobody. The rule we settled on was that either a subscriber name or a company name is mandatory, and crucially the exact rule changed depending on context. Editing an existing service order had different constraints than creating one, because relaxing a field on edit must not corrupt records that were already valid under the old rule. Implementing that correctly meant the same idea had to be expressed consistently in three places. On the frontend, the Zod schema used a refinement, a cross-field rule that looks at several fields together and decides validity, so that if the personal name was empty the company name became required, and if both were empty the error appeared on both fields so the user could see exactly what was needed rather than guessing. On the backend, the GraphQL input had its own validation directives so that a malformed request was rejected at the edge regardless of what the client did, because you never trust the client to be the only line of defence. And the error had to travel cleanly from the backend rejection back to the specific frontend field through the shared error handler. I made a series of deliberate changes here, including relaxing subscriber validation to allow genuinely optional fields where the old rules were too strict, and making only the subscriber name or the company name mandatory on edit rather than over-constraining it. Each of those commits sounds tiny in isolation. Together they are a case study in conditional validation done properly. The lesson I took from it is that the hardest part of validation is rarely the regular expression. It is modelling a rule that genuinely depends on context and on other fields, expressing that same rule in more than one language without the two definitions drifting apart, and getting the resulting error to land in front of the user in a way that tells them precisely what to do next.

chapters.title: Performance and type safety
chapters.script: Two themes ran through years of my commits that are less visible than features but mattered as much, performance and type safety. The performance story I will tell is the event tables. Parts of Cortex Portal display long lists of events, network events and reporting events, and these lists can be very large. The original approach filtered and sorted on the frontend. That works with hundreds of rows and falls apart with many thousands. The browser has to receive everything, hold it in memory, and sort it on the main thread, and the interface stutters or freezes. The fix was to move searching and sorting to the backend. The query parameters grew a limit, a search term, and a sort, the resolvers did the work against the database where the data already lived and where indexes exist, and the frontend received only the page it needed. There was even a specific change to sort an event subject list on the backend rather than the client, for the same reason. This is a general principle worth stating plainly. Work belongs where the data is. Shipping a large dataset to the browser so the browser can throw most of it away is almost always the wrong design, and pushing the filter down to the store is almost always the right one. The type-safety theme was a long campaign rather than a single change. The goal was to remove the escape hatch type, the any type, which switches off TypeScript's checking wherever it appears, and to replace it with real types. The lever that made this tractable was code generation. Because the GraphQL schema generated TypeScript types, I could refactor forms and components to use those generated types instead of loose objects, which meant that a backend schema change would now break the frontend build loudly instead of failing silently at runtime in front of a user. There were many commits in this campaign, strongly typing form input names, using the generated types instead of restating shapes by hand, and then fixing the genuine errors that surfaced once the checking was actually on, because removing any always reveals real bugs that were hiding behind it. Alongside this I worked on the authorization pattern in the user interface itself. Rather than wrapping component bodies in nested conditionals, I moved to an early-return guard, where a component lacking permission returns nothing at the top and the rest of the component is the clear, unconditional happy path. None of these were features a customer would ever point at. All of them are the reason the codebase stayed fast and stayed honest as it grew.

chapters.title: Quality and security
chapters.script: The last theme is the one that does not show up in any user interface at all, quality and security, and it is the work I am quietest about and most serious about. On testing, the system had an end-to-end suite written with Playwright that drove a real browser through real journeys, creating and activating a new service, managing a subscriber, working support tickets. I did a lot of work keeping that suite meaningful through refactors and authentication changes, and I wrote the project's internal best-practices guide for it, roughly twenty patterns to follow and twenty anti-patterns to avoid, so that end-to-end tests, abbreviated as E2E, stayed reliable rather than becoming the flaky suite everyone learns to ignore. A flaky test suite is worse than no suite, because it trains a team to disbelieve red, and avoiding that outcome is a real engineering responsibility. Underneath that were Go fuzz tests, which throw deliberately malformed input at parsers to find crashes, and a body of integration tests that stood up real dependencies in containers and exercised them together rather than mocking everything into a comfortable lie. On security I did a steady stream of hardening that I want to describe concretely rather than vaguely. I prevented a path traversal vulnerability in document generation by validating that the resolved output directory actually stayed inside its intended parent, which stops a crafted name from escaping into the wider filesystem. I introduced a shared secure file permission constant so generated files were not created with overly permissive access, the weakness catalogued as insecure permissions. And I coordinated dependency upgrades across the monorepo when published vulnerabilities, the entries known as CVEs, landed in libraries we depended on, including bumping the browser automation framework to clear a specific advisory. None of this produced a demo. All of it is the difference between a system you can responsibly run for real customers and one you merely hope is fine. Looking back across the whole codebase, the through-line of my four years was consistency. Schema-first contracts so the layers could not silently disagree. A single validation framework so every form behaved the same way. Shared packages so two applications stayed one product. Generated types so a change broke the build instead of a customer. Tests and security work so none of it quietly rotted. The company is gone now, but the engineering discipline it took to keep a system this large coherent is the part I carry forward, and it is the part I would most want a team to know I can do again.

The contracts between services were shared, the code generation crossed language boundaries, and a monorepo let a single change to a schema ripple out to every consumer in one commit and one review. The backend was Go. The frontend was TypeScript and React. As a rough sense of scale, there were on the order of two hundred and forty thousand lines of Go and around eighty thousand lines of TypeScript, across roughly two thousand source files. That was split across five backend services, two main frontend applications, and a set of shared frontend packages. The backend services were the GraphQL portal interface, the network activator backend, the addressing service, a tenancy service that brokered database connections, and a collateral service that handled document storage. The frontends were the operator portal and the network activator application, with an administrative surface as well. The shared packages were published inside the workspace under a cortex scope. There was a validations package, a hooks package, a user interface component package, a utilities package, and a constants package. The point of those packages was that the two applications should not reinvent the same form validation, the same error handling, or the same design tokens independently. They should import them. The testing surface was substantial. There was an end-to-end suite written with Playwright, the browser automation framework, covering real user journeys like creating and activating a new service. There were Go fuzz tests, which feed deliberately malformed input into parsers to find crashes. There were integration tests that stood up real dependencies with containers, a database, the messaging system, and the portal interface, and exercised them together. And there was a continuous integration and delivery pipeline on GitLab that linted, vetted, tested, scanned for vulnerabilities, versioned, and built container images. None of those numbers are the interesting part on their own. What they tell you is that this was not a prototype. It was a system with enough surface area that consistency had to be engineered rather than hoped for, and most of my best work was about exactly that, making a large codebase behave like it was written by one careful person rather than many people in a hurry.

## The GraphQL core

The heart of the system was the portal interface, a Go service that exposed a single large GraphQL API. We used GraphQL deliberately. The frontend needed to compose very different views, an order list, a subscriber profile, a network summary, and a graph let each screen ask for exactly the data it needed without us hand-writing an endpoint per screen. The server was generated from the schema using gqlgen, a Go library that takes GraphQL schema files and produces the type-safe server scaffolding, leaving you to implement resolvers. There were dozens of schema files and a correspondingly large set of resolvers, organised by domain. There was an order resolver, a subscriber resolver, a named contact resolver, and so on. Each resolver was the place where business rules actually lived. Data lived in MongoDB, the document database, and here is where multi-tenancy showed up in the most concrete way. We did not have one shared database with a tenant column. Each tenant had its own database, and a connection manager component, which the code called connman, was responsible for handing a resolver the correct per-tenant connection based on the authenticated request. A resolver never picked a database. It asked the context for the tenant's connection and trusted that the plumbing had already isolated it. That design made cross-tenant data leakage structurally hard rather than merely discouraged. The service was also event-driven. It used the NATS messaging system, with messages defined as protocol buffers, to publish things that happened. When a user was updated, when an order changed state, the service published an event rather than calling every interested party directly. Other services subscribed. That decoupling let the activation workflows react to commercial events asynchronously without the portal interface knowing or caring who was listening. Startup of this service was itself a small lesson in real systems. It read configuration from the environment, registered tracing so requests could be followed across services, opened clients to the addressing, collateral, and tenancy services, established the messaging client with signature verification so forged events were rejected, set up a client for a carrier integration with mutual transport security, fetched the public keys needed to validate authentication tokens for every tenant, and then finally served traffic over a modern transport with a strict minimum security version. Every one of those steps existed because something in production needed it. The resolver code was the part people saw. The startup code was the part that kept it honest.

## The other services

The portal interface was the largest service but it was not alone, and the way the others were built is as informative as the way it was. The network activator backend was a representational state transfer API, a REST service, built on the Echo web framework in Go. It served the operations teams who drive provisioning. Its job was to expose endpoints for network configuration, to activate and erase services on devices, and to summarise orders and network state. It authenticated with the same token scheme as the portal but mapped each tenant to its identity pool, and it both published and consumed messaging events to coordinate asynchronous work. It is worth noticing that we did not force every service to be GraphQL. The activator was request-response and operational, so a plain REST API described from an OpenAPI specification fit it better. The addressing service was different again. It was a remote procedure call service using gRPC, Google's high-performance remote procedure call framework, and unlike the rest of the system its data lived in PostgreSQL, the relational database, not MongoDB. That choice was correct. Address and network topology data is highly relational and query-heavy, with postcodes, property identifiers, and network nodes, and a relational engine with real indexes is the right tool. The queries were not handwritten ad hoc. They were generated with sqlc, a tool that turns annotated SQL into type-safe Go functions, so the database layer was compile-checked rather than stringly typed. Schema changes were managed with versioned migrations. The tenancy service was small and almost boring on purpose. Its job was to broker per-tenant database connection details to the other services. There was even a tracked task to eventually remove it and fold its responsibility elsewhere, which tells you something healthy about the team. Infrastructure that exists only to glue other things together is a liability you should be looking to retire, not a monument. The collateral service handled document storage, uploads and generated paperwork, backed by object storage in the cloud. The reason this matters is the same reason the monorepo mattered. Each service was the right shape for its problem. GraphQL where views composed many entities, REST where the surface was operational, gRPC where it was tight service-to-service traffic over a relational store. Nobody was forced into a single pattern for ideological neatness, and the contracts between them were all generated from shared schemas so the freedom did not turn into chaos.

## Schema first development

If there is one idea that explains how this codebase stayed coherent at its size, it is schema-first development. Almost nothing important was written by hand twice. There were four kinds of contract, and each one generated code rather than being mirrored manually. GraphQL schema files generated the Go server types and resolver interfaces through gqlgen, and they also generated TypeScript types and React hooks for the frontend through a code generation toolchain. OpenAPI specifications generated the Go handlers and models for the REST services. Protocol buffer definitions generated the Go message types and the remote procedure call stubs. And annotated SQL generated the type-safe database access functions through sqlc. There was a generate step in the build that ran all of this in order, and a developer who changed a schema was expected to regenerate and commit the output. The reason this is worth a chapter of its own is the failure mode it removes. In a hand-synchronised system, the backend changes a field, the frontend keeps the old shape, and nothing complains until a user hits the bug in production. In a schema-first system the same change breaks the build. The TypeScript stops compiling because the generated type changed. The Go stops compiling because the resolver signature changed. The mismatch is caught at the moment it is introduced, by the person who introduced it, on their own machine, instead of by a customer weeks later. There was also a quieter benefit that I leaned on heavily in my own work. Because the frontend types were generated from the same schema as the backend, I could derive form field names and input shapes directly from the generated types instead of typing string literals. When the schema renamed a field, every form that referenced it failed to compile until it was fixed. That turned a whole class of silent runtime bugs into loud compile-time bugs. Generated code has a reputation for being ugly, and some of it was. The honest tradeoff is that you accept large generated files in version control and a slightly slower build in exchange for an entire category of integration mistake simply not being possible. On a system with this many moving parts and more than one author, that trade was overwhelmingly worth making. A great deal of my time was spent making sure the generation pipeline was actually trusted, because a code generation step that people route around by hand is worse than none at all.

## Authorization and input safety

Security in Cortex Portal was not a separate module bolted on the side. It was expressed in the schema and enforced by the framework on every single request, and that is a design I came to strongly believe in. Authorization used a custom GraphQL directive. Every query and mutation that needed protection was annotated in the schema with a has-permission directive listing the permissions required, written in a resource and action style, for example read on the order resource or update on the subscriber resource. A piece of middleware implemented that directive. Before a resolver ran, the middleware compared the permissions on the authenticated request against the permissions the field declared, and if they did not match it returned an authorization error and the resolver never executed. The important property is that authorization was declarative and lived next to the field it protected, so you could read the schema and see exactly who was allowed to do what, rather than hunting through imperative checks scattered across the code. Input validation worked the same way. There was a validate directive that applied tag-based rules to input fields, things like required, or a valid email, or a value greater than zero, with custom messages. There was a validate-regex directive for pattern rules, which is how that strict carrier appointment identifier format was enforced at the edge. And there was an html directive for the rare fields that legitimately accept formatted text, like a notification body. That directive ran the input through a sanitiser using the bluemonday library with a user-generated-content policy, which strips dangerous markup and prevents cross-site scripting, the class of attack abbreviated as XSS where attacker markup runs in another user's browser. I did a meaningful amount of the work on this surface. I added the safe html scalar type and its directive, and I fixed real bugs in it, like trimming whitespace so a trailing newline from a text area did not defeat validation. The mental model I want to leave you with is this. The schema was the single place that described not just the shape of the data but the rules about it. Who can call this. What must be true about the input. What gets sanitised. Because all of that was declarative and enforced centrally, a new resolver was secure by default. You had to actively annotate it to open it up, rather than remembering to add protection you could easily forget. Secure-by-default is worth far more than secure-if-you-remember.

## Multi tenant isolation

Multi-tenancy is easy to say and hard to do correctly, and Cortex Portal took the stricter path. Every internet service provider on the platform, every ISP, was a tenant, and tenants had to be isolated so completely that one provider could never see another provider's subscribers, orders, or addresses, even through a bug. Identity was handled by a managed cloud authentication service. Each tenant had its own user pool, its own population of users entirely separate from every other tenant. When a user signed in, the token they received carried the tenant context. The portal interface fetched the configuration for every tenant's pool and maintained the set of public keys needed to verify tokens, per pool, so a token could be both authenticated and attributed to the right tenant on every request. Data isolation was physical rather than logical. Instead of one shared database with a tenant identifier column on every table, which is the design where a single missing filter leaks everyone's data, each tenant had its own MongoDB database. The connection manager I mentioned earlier resolved the right database from the request's tenant and placed that connection in the request context. Resolvers read the connection from context. They did not, and structurally could not, choose a different tenant's database by forgetting a filter, because there was no shared store to forget to filter. The one place data was deliberately shared was the addressing service on PostgreSQL, where geography is genuinely common across tenants, and there isolation was enforced explicitly in the query layer. Standing a tenant up was not just a database. A new tenant needed baseline data to be usable at all. Roles had to exist, an administrator role with full permissions, an operator role, a tenant user role. Permissions had to be attached to those roles. Product offerings, order status values, and activity types had to be present. There was a seeding system that produced this consistent baseline, and I did a lot of work there, adding permissions for new resources to the right roles, seeding prospect and subscriber templates, and fixing the not-found handling around them. Seed data sounds trivial until you realise that every developer environment, every test run, and every freshly created tenant depends on it being correct and consistent. If the seed is wrong, every downstream test is testing the wrong world. Getting that boring layer right is what lets the exciting layers be trustworthy.

## The frontend

The frontend was a TypeScript and React codebase, and it was built with the same seriousness as the backend rather than treated as a thin skin over the API. The main applications used React version eighteen, with React Router for navigation and Apollo Client as the GraphQL client, which gave us a normalised cache and generated hooks for every operation. The component library was Ant Design, a mature enterprise component system, which was the right call for software whose users are operations staff filling in dense forms all day rather than consumers browsing a marketing site. Styling used Emotion, a library for writing component-scoped styles in TypeScript. The build tool was Rsbuild, a modern fast bundler. The detail that mattered most was the shared packages under the cortex scope. There was a validations package holding reusable rules, things like a valid United Kingdom phone number, a valid service identifier, password strength, names. There was a hooks package with cross-application React hooks. There was a user interface package wrapping the component system with consistent theming and layout primitives. There was a utilities package, and a constants package holding error codes and shared strings. The reason this structure existed is that we had more than one application. Without shared packages, the portal and the network activator would each grow their own slightly different phone number validator and their own slightly different error display, and they would drift apart and both be subtly wrong. With shared packages there was exactly one phone number validator, tested once, used everywhere. I spent real effort consolidating things into that shared layer. One concrete example was icons. Early on, components imported icons from several different libraries in several different ways, which bloated the bundle and made the interface visually inconsistent. I built a single icon map that exported every icon the applications used, and then methodically migrated component after component to reference it, so there was one source of truth and one bundle cost. Another example was layout. The same flex container with the same gap was written by hand in dozens of components. I extracted small layout utilities, a flex gap helper, a header row helper, and replaced the duplication. None of this is glamorous. Nobody demos an icon map. But this kind of consolidation is the difference between a frontend that gets faster and more consistent as it grows and one that gets slower and more random. A large React codebase does not stay coherent by accident. It stays coherent because someone keeps deliberately pulling the shared parts back into the centre, and on this project that someone was frequently me.

## The validation framework

The piece of Cortex Portal I owned most completely was the form and validation framework on the frontend, and it is the part I would most want to be asked about. Cortex Portal is, from the user's seat, an enormous collection of forms. Create a subscriber. Edit a service order. Configure a tenant application. Add a named contact. Every one of those is a form with rules, and rules that are wrong or inconsistent are not cosmetic. They block real orders or let bad data through. I architected the validation layer around two libraries working together. React Hook Form managed form state and submission efficiently, and Zod described the shape and rules of the data as a schema. The pattern was that each form defined a Zod schema once, and from that single schema we derived both the runtime validation, which actually rejects bad input, and the static TypeScript type of the form values. One declaration, two guarantees, always in step. That sounds clean stated in one sentence. The reality was a long, careful migration spanning months. The validation had started as ad hoc rules, and moving more than fifty forms onto declarative schemas without breaking live workflows was incremental surgery. On top of that I led two non-trivial dependency migrations underneath the framework, moving the schema library from its third major version to its fourth, whose syntax changed, and moving the form resolver bridge from its third major version to its fifth. Those upgrades touched every form, so they had to be done methodically, with the type checker and the test suite as the safety net rather than hope. The part I am proudest of is error handling, because that is where most form systems quietly fail. A server can reject input the client thought was fine, a duplicate value for instance. If that error just appears as a generic toast, the user has no idea which field to fix. I built a shared error handler hook that took a server error, extracted the field path from the error's structured extensions, recognised specific codes like a duplicate, and set the message on exactly the right form field with a helpful message, falling back gracefully when it could not. The result was that a backend rejection turned into a red message under the precise input that caused it, not a vague banner. That single piece of plumbing, unglamorous as it is, probably removed more daily user frustration than any feature I shipped.

## Subscribers and named contacts

I want to tell one story in detail, because it shows how a small-sounding rule reaches through every layer of a real system. In Cortex Portal a subscriber is the customer on a broadband order, and a named contact is an authorised representative tied to that subscriber, someone allowed to act on the account. The deceptively hard rule was identity. Sometimes the customer is a person, with a first name and a last name. Sometimes the customer is a company, with a company name and no personal name. The system could not demand both, because for a residential customer there is no company, and it could not demand neither, because then you have an order attached to nobody. The rule we settled on was that either a subscriber name or a company name is mandatory, and crucially the exact rule changed depending on context. Editing an existing service order had different constraints than creating one, because relaxing a field on edit must not corrupt records that were already valid under the old rule. Implementing that correctly meant the same idea had to be expressed consistently in three places. On the frontend, the Zod schema used a refinement, a cross-field rule that looks at several fields together and decides validity, so that if the personal name was empty the company name became required, and if both were empty the error appeared on both fields so the user could see exactly what was needed rather than guessing. On the backend, the GraphQL input had its own validation directives so that a malformed request was rejected at the edge regardless of what the client did, because you never trust the client to be the only line of defence. And the error had to travel cleanly from the backend rejection back to the specific frontend field through the shared error handler. I made a series of deliberate changes here, including relaxing subscriber validation to allow genuinely optional fields where the old rules were too strict, and making only the subscriber name or the company name mandatory on edit rather than over-constraining it. Each of those commits sounds tiny in isolation. Together they are a case study in conditional validation done properly. The lesson I took from it is that the hardest part of validation is rarely the regular expression. It is modelling a rule that genuinely depends on context and on other fields, expressing that same rule in more than one language without the two definitions drifting apart, and getting the resulting error to land in front of the user in a way that tells them precisely what to do next.

## Performance and type safety

Two themes ran through years of my commits that are less visible than features but mattered as much, performance and type safety. The performance story I will tell is the event tables. Parts of Cortex Portal display long lists of events, network events and reporting events, and these lists can be very large. The original approach filtered and sorted on the frontend. That works with hundreds of rows and falls apart with many thousands. The browser has to receive everything, hold it in memory, and sort it on the main thread, and the interface stutters or freezes. The fix was to move searching and sorting to the backend. The query parameters grew a limit, a search term, and a sort, the resolvers did the work against the database where the data already lived and where indexes exist, and the frontend received only the page it needed. There was even a specific change to sort an event subject list on the backend rather than the client, for the same reason. This is a general principle worth stating plainly. Work belongs where the data is. Shipping a large dataset to the browser so the browser can throw most of it away is almost always the wrong design, and pushing the filter down to the store is almost always the right one. The type-safety theme was a long campaign rather than a single change. The goal was to remove the escape hatch type, the any type, which switches off TypeScript's checking wherever it appears, and to replace it with real types. The lever that made this tractable was code generation. Because the GraphQL schema generated TypeScript types, I could refactor forms and components to use those generated types instead of loose objects, which meant that a backend schema change would now break the frontend build loudly instead of failing silently at runtime in front of a user. There were many commits in this campaign, strongly typing form input names, using the generated types instead of restating shapes by hand, and then fixing the genuine errors that surfaced once the checking was actually on, because removing any always reveals real bugs that were hiding behind it. Alongside this I worked on the authorization pattern in the user interface itself. Rather than wrapping component bodies in nested conditionals, I moved to an early-return guard, where a component lacking permission returns nothing at the top and the rest of the component is the clear, unconditional happy path. None of these were features a customer would ever point at. All of them are the reason the codebase stayed fast and stayed honest as it grew.

## Quality and security

The last theme is the one that does not show up in any user interface at all, quality and security, and it is the work I am quietest about and most serious about. On testing, the system had an end-to-end suite written with Playwright that drove a real browser through real journeys, creating and activating a new service, managing a subscriber, working support tickets. I did a lot of work keeping that suite meaningful through refactors and authentication changes, and I wrote the project's internal best-practices guide for it, roughly twenty patterns to follow and twenty anti-patterns to avoid, so that end-to-end tests, abbreviated as E2E, stayed reliable rather than becoming the flaky suite everyone learns to ignore. A flaky test suite is worse than no suite, because it trains a team to disbelieve red, and avoiding that outcome is a real engineering responsibility. Underneath that were Go fuzz tests, which throw deliberately malformed input at parsers to find crashes, and a body of integration tests that stood up real dependencies in containers and exercised them together rather than mocking everything into a comfortable lie. On security I did a steady stream of hardening that I want to describe concretely rather than vaguely. I prevented a path traversal vulnerability in document generation by validating that the resolved output directory actually stayed inside its intended parent, which stops a crafted name from escaping into the wider filesystem. I introduced a shared secure file permission constant so generated files were not created with overly permissive access, the weakness catalogued as insecure permissions. And I coordinated dependency upgrades across the monorepo when published vulnerabilities, the entries known as CVEs, landed in libraries we depended on, including bumping the browser automation framework to clear a specific advisory. None of this produced a demo. All of it is the difference between a system you can responsibly run for real customers and one you merely hope is fine. Looking back across the whole codebase, the through-line of my four years was consistency. Schema-first contracts so the layers could not silently disagree. A single validation framework so every form behaved the same way. Shared packages so two applications stayed one product. Generated types so a change broke the build instead of a customer. Tests and security work so none of it quietly rotted. The company is gone now, but the engineering discipline it took to keep a system this large coherent is the part I carry forward, and it is the part I would most want a team to know I can do again.
